01 / The whole system

How your
backtest works.

The program uses saved company data and prices to select stocks. It then checks how those stocks performed.

This guide explains each part, how the parts connect, and why some runs take longer. You do not need to read the code.

Saved dataOne set of selection rulesFour ways to use itNo downloads during a backtest

The main data flow

Save once. Prepare once.
Select many times.

A cache is saved data that the program can use again. Select a step to see its job.

1. The source data stays on your computer.

The raw folder holds the saved inputs. Ordinary preparation and backtests read these files. They do not contact the data supplier.

The browser and Python use the same selection rules. They use different prepared records for different dates.

02 / Three ways to use it

The date choice sets the path.

Latest picks work in the saved HTML page. Custom dates and random dates need the local Python service. A January study is a custom schedule every 12 months from 1 January; there is no January mode.

Choose when the test runs.

Clear Auto-run when settings change to edit several settings before a run. Then select Run backtest, or Screen latest in latest mode. The browser remembers this choice. Reset buttons and stock-count presets also respect it.

An amber notice appears when the displayed results differ from the current settings. It clears after a successful matching run or when you restore the result’s settings. Charts, stock lists and downloads keep the last successful result until a new run finishes. A failed or stopped run does not replace that result.

Custom and random backtests run on the server. Locking your phone, refreshing, closing the page or changing views does not stop the calculation. Reopen the same address in the same browser to retrieve progress or the completed result. The browser stores each run ID before submission. It also records server acceptance and Stop intent. A refresh before acceptance retries the same ID. After acceptance, reconnection retrieves the existing run. Recovery checks each saved run against current server status. It selects active work first. Otherwise, it selects the newest available completed result. Failed, stopped and expired runs are skipped. A rejected submission in another tab does not remove the active run’s recovery record.

You can edit settings during a backtest. Those edits do not change its submitted settings. They do not queue another run. Select Stop backtest to request cancellation. If disconnected, the page retries that request when it reconnects. The controls stay busy until the server confirms cleanup. Completed random trials stay cached. An unfinished trial is rolled back. Active workers finish their current books before cleanup releases cache ownership.

Keep the server computer awake and its terminal open. One backtest can run on each server at a time. Temporary results stay in server memory for 24 hours, up to four recent runs. They disappear when the server exits. Use Save displayed backtest to keep a completed result in the library. Recovery needs the same browser storage and website address. Stopping the server cancels active work and waits for cleanup.

These controls are in the current source. Installing a committed revision and reloading the page makes them available in the native website. Source edits do not change an already running server.

How do I queue tests for an overnight run?

Select Add to queue beside Run backtest. From latest mode, the first click opens the dated backtest settings. It turns off Auto-run and starts no calculation. Set a fixed or random-date test, then select Add to queue again. Use View queue to open the list below the strategy controls. You can enter an optional name there before adding a test. Change the settings to add another test. Auto-run is suspended while the queue has waiting or running work. Adding, copying or editing a queue item also clears the Auto-run checkbox. This keeps setup manual between fast cached tests. Explicit Run backtest remains available.

Tests run one at a time. You can close this page or lock your phone. Keep the server computer awake and its terminal open. A failed test remains visible and does not stop the next test.

Select Edit settings to hold a waiting test. Use the strategy controls to change its parameters. Save to return it to the queue, or cancel to keep its previous settings. Moving this test or its neighbor does not invalidate the edit. Each edit has an identity and a settings version. The server keeps its latest Save or Cancel receipt. An exact retry stays safe after the test starts. If a response is lost, the page checks the receipt or offers a retry. If another browser ends or replaces the hold, the form becomes available and keeps its current settings. Held edits stay held after a page or server restart. Use Release hold to return an abandoned edit to the queue. Running settings cannot change. While an edit owns the form, opening a queue or library result, copying another test, or recovering a manual run cannot replace its draft. Save or cancel the edit first. The same form check protects all settings restoration paths.

Move up and Move down change waiting order. Copy settings loads parameters for a new test. Pause queue lets the active test finish and prevents the next test from starting. Stop test cancels the selected active test. The next test waits for worker and cache cleanup.

Select Open result to restore stored charts, all trial stocks and downloads. No calculation runs. Completed results move to Saved backtests automatically. A full library shows Completed — waiting for saved slot. Other save failures keep the complete result in the queue and show a retry notice. The server retries without recalculation, including while execution is paused or the engine is unavailable. The library checks prior transfer receipts and free slots before copying a result. It checks both again when it saves. Failed and stopped tests remain here. Deletion confirms one selected record. Stop a running test before deleting it. During a transfer, refresh and retry deletion after it finishes.

The queue holds up to 100 records that are still visible. Successful transfers free queue slots. It uses data/backtest-queue.sqlite. Keep this durable file during preparation, cleanup and deployment. The queue is separate from temporary immediate runs and the 100-slot saved library. The saved copy commits before duplicate queue result bytes are removed. There is no automatic eviction.

One consumer lock protects queue execution across server instances. Queue transactions end before financial ownership starts. A manual backtest or data rebuild can delay queue work. It does not turn waiting tests into lock-timeout failures. Shutdown waits for normal engine cleanup and returns unfinished work to the queue. A successor recovers running records only after it owns the consumer lock. Stop intent remains cancelled.

A random seed is stored at admission. The full trial date plan is stored before calculation and reused after interruption. Changing waiting calculation parameters discards the old plan. Renaming a test keeps its dates. Tests use saved financial inputs available when they execute. Completed artifacts keep their original priced results.

How do I keep a completed backtest?

Select Save displayed backtest. You can enter a name first. The record keeps the settings used for that result, all traded stocks and all returns. Pending setting edits are not included. A failed or stopped run does not replace the completed result.

Open Manage saved backtests to find a record. Select Open to restore its settings, charts, stock tables and CSV downloads. No calculation runs. Later data changes do not rewrite saved results. Saved metric labels, filter labels and warnings also stay with the original result. Earlier saved records still open without changing their stored data.

A saved January result opens in the dated view. Its book years become dated periods when it is read. Period dates that were not stored show the book year. The stored record is not rewritten, and saving it again sends the stored record. The results notice says that no current setting reproduces it.

Select Copy settings on a saved row to load its parameters into the current strategy controls. Adjust the controls, then select Run backtest. Copying turns off Auto-run and starts no calculation. The displayed result keeps its original values. The editable controls keep the copied test’s labels. A saved choice that is no longer supported stays visible as unavailable. Custom formulas retain their captured revisions and labels. Random dates restore the recorded seed for repeatable tuning. Save or cancel a held queue edit before copying another test.

A random-date record includes every trial’s trade dates, traded stocks and period returns. It also keeps the seed and distribution summary. Trial inspection reads these saved stocks. It does not recalculate a book.

The library has 100 slots. When all slots are used, delete a chosen record before saving another. The program never removes an older record to make room. Deletion asks for confirmation. The displayed result stays available after its saved record is deleted.

Each record shows its stable UUID database ID. Select Rename, enter a name, then select Save name or Cancel. Renaming changes only the name. It keeps the ID, creation date, settings and all result bytes. Automatic queue updates wait until you finish renaming, so they do not interrupt typing.

Use Sort saved backtests to show the newest saved records, highest performance first, or lowest performance first. Performance means CAGR for January and fixed dates. It means mean trial CAGR for random dates. Different windows and test types can differ. Missing performance stays last. Equal values use the saved date and ID for a stable order.

The queue and library lists scroll inside bounded regions. Their headings and controls remain outside the lists. Keyboard users can focus each list and scroll it.

A successful save, rename or deletion stays confirmed if a later list refresh fails. The page keeps the confirmed change in its list. Select Refresh saved list to check records from other browser sessions. Do not repeat an already confirmed save.

Each saved row has an All parameters disclosure. Expand it to read that test’s recorded settings and selected filters. This does not open its result or change the strategy form. The first expansion loads only that record. Loading feedback appears in the row. A failed load shows Retry parameters. Sorting, renaming and refreshing keep the expansion. Deleted records clear their cached descriptions. Temporary evidence readers close after the parameter rows are read.

Choose First saved test and Second saved test, then select Compare. Choose two different IDs. Recorded performance and parameter tables appear inside the library. Amber rows also show the word Different. Sorting and renaming preserve the selected IDs. Deleting a selected record clears its comparison. Clear comparison clears both choices. The main result and strategy form stay unchanged.

Comparison reads stored results without recalculation. Legacy and current calendars compare in one form. Documented omission defaults keep their meaning. Reordering AND conditions or repeating an identical condition changes no result. Strict operators, exact values, unknown settings and stored labels remain visible. Requested engine and recorded producer are separate. An older result without producer evidence stays unidentified. Random tests show requested seed policy, the recorded seed and stored trial statistics. Mean trial CAGR is not one portfolio return. Percentiles are not confidence intervals. Notices identify different test types, requested windows and recorded observation windows.

Comparison tables scroll inside a bounded keyboard-accessible region. Temporary evidence readers are released after compact descriptions are read. A changed selection or Clear discards late comparison replies without changing the main result.

Queue transfers save one independent record per completed test. A durable import receipt prevents duplicates after interruption. The receipt survives saved-record deletion. Recovery keeps later renames and explicit deletion. Archived queue receipts cannot restart or redisplay old tests. Existing open result readers keep their original bytes when duplicate queue storage is released.

Records live on the server computer in data/saved-backtests.sqlite. Browser sessions using that runtime share the library. The records survive browser restarts, server restarts and prepared-cache rebuilds. Keep this file when you clean caches. Back it up with your user data. A saved HTML page needs the local service to use the library.

Prepared in advance · Runs in the browser

A screen for the latest saved session.

Prepared latest records→Data inside the HTML→Browser selection→Stock list

Latest means the latest SPY session in the saved data. It does not mean a live market feed.

A company needs a price on that exact session. The saved company list must mark it as listed. Old stopped prices are excluded. These picks have no future holding return.

Prepared when needed · Uses the local Python service

A test on your chosen calendar.

Browser request→Local Python service→Saved or new dated books→Results in the browser

Choose the start date, end date and rebalance interval. Opening this view runs nothing by itself. Original runs this test. It supports the 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24-month presets and custom 1–104 weeks or 1–24 months.

Trade dates move forward to a saved SPY session. The end mark moves back to a session. A new buy/sell date pair usually needs a new book. A saved pair can be reused.

A request for the removed January mode fails with UNSUPPORTED_CAPABILITY at /mode. It is never converted to a dated schedule.

Many dated tests · Uses the local Python service

The same strategy on different trade dates.

Sample trade dates→Calculate with Original→Calculate complete trials→Save and recover completed trials→Compare trial results

For each trial, the program selects one trading session from each frequency block. The last partial block also participates. Actual holding periods can have different lengths.

Trials use the same start and end window. Strategy and SPY hold cash until the first trade. Original plans shared missing date pairs and calculates books ahead. One parent saves completed trials and presents them in recorded order.

New runs use fresh dates by default. A seed is a number that lets you repeat the date choices. Use the same saved settings and seed to replay a batch.

What happens when you double-click start.cmd?

Run backtest-web.cmd in Windows Terminal, or double-click start.cmd. The website stays attached to this terminal on 0.0.0.0:3000. Open http://127.0.0.1:3000 on this computer. The terminal shows server logs. Press Ctrl+C to stop. A new launch stops this project’s identified server and starts current code in the new terminal. This also replaces an older background instance. A startup lock serializes preparation and binding. A lifetime lock stays held until the listener and all request threads close. A stopped HTTP endpoint does not release ownership. A replacement waits up to 30 seconds, then asks you to wait or stop the old terminal and retry. Python prepares stale caches and builds before it opens the browser. A launch serves the installed revision and never updates by itself. The terminal checks committed main once a day at 01:00 local time. A new commit then deploys and restarts the server after cleanup. Many commits in one day cause one restart. Add --latest to install the newest main commit at launch. Uncommitted saves do not trigger updates. An unrelated port owner is left running; the website uses a free port.

Development and runtime

Edit in WSL.
Run native Windows code.

The WSL source checkout owns code and Git history. The Windows runtime owns saved market data, prepared databases, logs and local builds.

WSL source→Committed source deployment→Windows runtime

From WSL, run python3 tools/deploy.py --start. From Windows Terminal, run the installed backtest-web.cmd. The WSL launcher starts the installed revision with native Windows Python in that terminal. It checks main once a day at 01:00 local time. A new commit then deploys and restarts the server. Run backtest-web.cmd --latest to install the newest main commit at launch. A fresh runtime installs main. Uncommitted edits and linked worktrees are excluded. The source checkout is . The runtime is . The original legacy folder remains a fallback.

The source launcher locates tools/deploy.py relative to its command file. It can run from the WSL network path without changing CMD’s working directory. This fix stays in source until a committed revision containing it is installed.

What does deployment change?

Deployment publishes one exact Git commit. Normal server startup serves the installed revision and follows committed main at 01:00 daily. Standalone publication and --check retain the installed commit from data/deployment.json. A fresh standalone publication requires an explicit revision; automatic startup selects main only with --latest, at the daily check or on a fresh runtime. Use python3 tools/deploy.py --revision <commit> --start from WSL to select a fixed revision without automatic updates. An explicit --revision HEAD fixes that launch to the resolved commit. It does not qualify an experimental engine. Working-tree edits stay in WSL. The runtime has no separate Git repository. Source file hashes and the deployed commit are recorded in data/deployment.json. Only source files owned by the preceding deployment can be removed. Unexpected source edits or conflicting local files stop publication.

Raw data, databases, environments, logs, the local website build and baseline revision history stay on Windows. The runtime copy of the January report also stays there. Deployment never installs, replaces or removes that file, and nothing reads it. The tracked report is a frozen record. No command collects a runtime report into source.

How are running servers protected?

The entry point website/serve.py takes shared source ownership before importing website/server/app.py. It holds ownership through server cleanup. website/runtime_access.py owns this boundary. Deployment stops authenticated instances from this runtime, including alternate ports. It waits for process exit, then takes exclusive source ownership and financial cache ownership. Unknown listeners remain running.

An interrupted source publication leaves data/deployment.pending.json. Startup refuses to import the application while that journal exists. Run deployment again to finish the verified publication. Default retry selects the journal’s commit. It does not restore the older manifest commit after recovery. An explicit different revision is rejected before staging. Finish recovery before selecting another revision. Do not remove the journal to bypass recovery.

Automatic updates watch committed main in the registered WSL source. They do not fetch Git history. A source archive is ready before the old child receives its private stop marker. The server performs normal Ctrl+C cleanup, including during startup preparation. Deployment waits for the child to exit, then keeps the existing source and financial lock order. Active manual runs stop. Interrupted queued tests return to waiting with their recorded dates. Saved results and raw data stay in place. A missing Git observation keeps the current server. Failed updates retry automatically and preserve pending recovery. Ctrl+C stops this watcher and its own server. A server replaced by another terminal ends its old watcher. Refresh an open browser page after the new server is ready. Automatic restarts do not open another tab.

What does the development log record?

Each server process writes its own log in data/logs/website-<namespace>-<pid>.log. The data panel shows its path. Each line is one JSON event with a UTC time. The log never contains exception text, source lines, local variables, keys, provider URLs or response bodies. A failure keeps its error types, OS codes and stack locations. The logs stay local and are excluded from Git. Server and update-watcher lines in the terminal start with the local date and time. The three lines of a website build do not.

A long operation writes one event when it ends. The event gives the outcome, the wall seconds, the CPU seconds of the operation’s thread, stage seconds and counts. backtest.run covers each manual or queued calculation. It records the mode, the admission, the pool, the number of periods and trials, and the book statistics of random trials. Its stages include the admission wait, planning, book calculation, book writes, selection and result sealing. queue.test adds the result store time and the reason for a requeue. prepare.research records each preparation phase and the number of cached companies. Every research build is a full build. prepare.daily records the copied and parsed price files and the kept books. startup.prepare and data.job cover startup and data-panel work. A request that takes one second or more writes http.slow with its route. The route has no identifiers and no query text.

Stages are measured regions. They can overlap, so they need not add up to the total seconds.

An operation that takes longer than one minute also reports progress. After its first minute, it writes a running line, and then one more every five minutes. The line gives the time so far, the last finished step and the time since it, the stage in progress when one is open, live counts and the process CPU time. A report also counts for the operations around the reporter, which it names, for example startup and the daily cache around the research database. An operation with an open inner operation waits one more minute, so a long inner operation reports for it. An operation made of short inner operations then reports for itself. When a reporting operation ends, the operation around it reports at once, so the latest progress line stays current. A step of one minute or more writes a step line when it ends. A step that only waited for an inner operation writes no step line, because that operation’s end line already shows its time. An operation that ends within a minute writes only its end line. If a process stops during an operation, its last progress line shows where it was.

Run python3 -m tools.ops.log_summary from the project folder. It first lists unfinished operations with their latest progress line. Then it prints the median, 90th-percentile and longest time of each operation, its largest stage shares, the latest backtest runs, slow requests and failures. Add --days 7 to read only the last week. Reading never changes a log.

A log rotates at 5 MiB and keeps two older files. Startup removes logs that have had no write for 14 days. Then it removes the oldest logs of stopped servers in this process namespace until those logs total at most 50 files and 100 MiB. The file name holds the namespace: machine identity on Windows, boot and PID namespace on Linux, so a Linux reboot starts a new namespace. A log from another namespace or an older name format has no process to check. Only its age removes it, and it does not count toward these targets. When the namespace is unknown, only age applies. The log of a running server in this namespace stays, and so does a file that cannot be deleted. Cleanup errors never stop startup.

Where do tests run?

WSL runs source and synthetic checks. python3 tools/deploy.py --check deploys committed code and runs the installed Windows checks, including saved-data path checks, preparation and browser parity. It does not download market data. Each operating system has its own environment and compiled caches.

03 / One holding period

From a report to a portfolio.

A book describes one buy date and one sell or mark date. The dated engine prepares the requested stock group before it applies your final filters.

  1. Choose a usable annual report.

    The report becomes available 90 days after its year-end. Availability must be before the buy date. A report older than 800 days is excluded.

  2. Prepare the requested stock group.

    The original group keeps the original 250-name screen. The broader group uses companies with saved prices. Only the requested group is prepared. Neither group covers the full market.

  3. Estimate values at the buy date.

    The program uses saved prices to update report market cap. It adds report net debt to estimate enterprise value. A missing buy price excludes a stock.

  4. Prepare metrics and holding returns.

    The program calculates both supported EBITDA metrics for the requested group. It uses dividend-adjusted prices for holding returns. It saves these records for the date pair.

  5. Apply the chosen selection order.

    The program reads your chosen group. Filter first is the default. It applies all conditions, ranks the matches and takes the requested ranks. Rank first takes the requested ranks before applying all conditions. It keeps original ranks and adds no replacements. Lower selected EV/EBITDA multiples rank first.

  6. Calculate the portfolio result.

    Each selected stock starts with the same weight. The program averages their holding returns. It joins the periods and compares the result with SPY.

Period return = sum of selected stock returns ÷ actual selected stock count
What if a stock stops trading?

The historical engine uses its last available price. The proceeds stay as cash until the next rebalance. A listed bankruptcy override gives a total loss. Each override names a stock and the day of the loss. Only a book whose window contains that day takes the loss: after the entry day, through the exit day. The override list is currently empty.

Each holding shows how it exited. A normal exit shows Scheduled exit. The last period of a test shows Marked to date when it ends on the test's end date and not on a scheduled rebalance. Random and explicit trades always end that way. Last available price and Bankruptcy keep their labels. A saved book is shared by every schedule with the same dates, so the test applies the final label, not the book. Saved results keep the labels that they were saved with.

A later delisting does not change an earlier sale price. The original review covered 37 early stops. Additional stops in expanded or dated tests have not all received that review.

How are complete dated results calculated?

Fixed and explicit-date tests use one portfolio reducer in backtest/portfolio_results.py. It keeps all selected stock rows in rank order. Equal weights use the actual stock count. Signed contributions, period compounding, stopped proceeds and cash before the first trade keep their existing meaning. An empty period makes strategy growth and CAGR unavailable. SPY remains visible.

The website obtains books through daily SQLite preparation and the shared SQL selector. The reducer can also emit one complete period at a time. A separate versioned evidence codec writes bounded pieces to caller-owned files. It preserves all holdings and original metadata. Partial writes never become completed trials. Oversized recorded plans use a fixed private file with a separate 16 MiB limit. Full plan validation precedes calculation. Existing Jobs can own a temporary completed copy, byte reservations and pinned readers. Expiry ends new access; open readers keep their bytes until closure.

Explicit version-3 operations copy complete evidence into the existing queue and saved-library databases. Each record owns ordered 64 KiB chunks. One transaction validates and publishes every byte and the original settings and labels. A failed copy preserves the source and earlier records. Opening creates a charged temporary reader and closes the database before returning it. Deleting the stored record cannot invalidate that reader. The library and the queue each keep a 100-record cap. The queue also keeps Stop precedence and mutation receipts. Old version-1/2 records are not rewritten. The additive browser reader now opens version 3 through the same ResultArtifacts boundary as fresh results. Automatic submission and queue execution remain eager. Their limits are unchanged. Read the bounded evidence contract and durable snapshot contract for their limits.

Financial result contract version 1 lives in evidence headers. Existing jobs and saved results gain no required fields. Dates, status strings, nulls, ordered holdings, weights and contribution values stay complete. Daily-cache freshness includes the reducer source. This does not update a running server. Read the complete financial result contract for fields and limits.

Which calendar intervals does the source support?

Original supports the 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24-month presets and custom 1–104 weeks and 1–24 months. Fixed and random planners share backtest/calendar.py. Version 1 configurations keep interval unit and count explicit. Custom controls follow the server engine capability. Direct-file pages cannot execute dated runs. This source change does not update an installed server.

Each target uses the original start date. A week has seven calendar days. Monthly targets clamp to the last day of the destination month. Fixed targets roll forward to saved sessions. Duplicate rolled targets merge. The inclusive end mark rolls back. Random trials sample one session in each nonempty nominal block. A final partial block participates when it contains a session. Empty blocks consume no random draw. Explicit trades use the same window without an interval. Daily-cache freshness includes the calendar source. Artifact and financial interface versions stay the same. Canonical results retain the requested calendar and resolved session dates separately. Legacy month results keep their original fields. Random replay sends the recorded date plan. Saved results keep original settings and labels. Canonical random CSV files identify interval unit and count. Opening or exporting a saved result does not calculate. Read the calendar API and compatibility rules for the exact contract.

What if too few stocks pass the screen?

The program uses the stocks that pass. If 80 stocks pass a top-100 request, each starts with a weight of 1/80.

An empty holding period makes full-window strategy growth and CAGR unavailable. Random-date summaries keep incomplete trials visible. They exclude these trials from both paired distributions.

Which financial values are used?

The original saved annual record includes market cap, enterprise value and EV/EBITDA. Additional annual statement assets supply the financial ratio filters. The program derives EBITDA and net debt from those values.

Estimated EV equals estimated market cap plus report net debt. The three-year metric uses mean EBITDA from three consecutive annual reports. Missing years exclude the stock from that metric.

The 90-day delay is an availability assumption. It is not proof of the actual filing date. Supplier data can include later revisions.

04 / Groups, filters and counts

Three choices. Three different jobs.

The stock group sets where to look. Filters set which stocks can pass. The stock count sets how many to take.

The stock group / Pool

Where should the program look?

Original candidate set: the original 250-name screen, with its report-size rules. Missing prices can reduce the usable count.

All stocks with cached prices: a broader saved-price group. It is still a partial market universe.

Filters and stock count

Which stocks, and how many?

Filters: market-cap bounds, minimum EV, selected metric yield, maximum multiple, sector and exchange. Add multiple conditions. Each one searches one list of built-in filters, saved variables, measures and parameters, then takes less than or more than and a value. Filter first is the default. All conditions must pass before ranking. Rank first selects the requested ranks before all conditions apply. Use two conditions on one item to set a range.

Count: top 50, top 100, or a rank range. Top 100 does not expand the original 250-name screen.

Explore a setting change · Filter-first examples only

Use the original candidate set. Apply your filters, rank the matching stocks, then take up to 50 stocks. Saved books for the same dates can be reused.

Choose when conditions apply.

Available conditions include market cap, enterprise value, both EV/EBITDA multiples, EBITDA/EV yield, and trailing 1-year and 3-year returns. Values use the units in each label: millions of dollars, percent, or multiples. Comparisons are strict. An equal value does not pass.

Trailing returns use dividend-adjusted closes on or before the screen date and its calendar anniversary. Each endpoint must be within seven calendar days. A leap-day anniversary clamps to 28 February. No future holding return is used. A missing value fails only a condition that needs it. Latest, custom and random views share these rules.

Selection order is shared by latest, fixed and random-date views. Filter first ranks only stocks that pass all user conditions. Rank first takes the requested ranks from the prepared stock group, then tests all user conditions on that shortlist. No replacements are added. If 20 stocks pass a top-50 shortlist, each receives 5% weight. Ranks can have gaps and keep their original numbers in stock lists and CSV files. A 10–20 request tests only those original 11 ranks. Prepared pool restrictions and missing ranking metrics still apply first.

Saved and queued tests keep the submitted order. Older saved records mean filter-first. Opening them does not rewrite or recalculate them. This choice is in current source. Source publication and an offline rebuild are needed before it appears in the installed website.

The saved books include these filter values. Changing conditions or selection order reuses the books. Source or input changes require offline preparation and a website rebuild. Reload an open page to use the new build.

Financial ratios use annual statement inputs.

Download Full annual financial data in Manage backtest data. This saves full provider responses for annual income statements, balance sheets, cash flow statements, key metrics and ratios for the chosen stock group. Every returned field is kept, including nulls, other currencies and filing metadata. Calculations select eligible USD inputs separately. The raw cache keeps fields for future metric calculations. Multiple records can have the same fiscal date. The raw cache keeps every returned row. For each numerical input, matching values can be used. Conflicting values stay unavailable. Response order does not select a revision. Then rebuild and reload the strategy page. Missing inputs exclude a stock only when a condition needs them.

P/E is screen-date market cap divided by annual net income. P/B uses annual stockholders’ equity. Free cash flow is shown in millions of USD. Its yield is free cash flow divided by screen-date market cap, in percent. Price/free cash flow uses the inverse ratio. Net profit margin is net income divided by revenue, in percent.

ROE uses net income divided by average stockholders’ equity from the selected and previous fiscal years, in percent. Both equity values must be positive. Current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. Interest coverage is EBIT divided by interest expense. Debt/equity is total debt divided by stockholders’ equity.

PEG is screen-date P/E divided by three-year diluted EPS compound annual growth, in percentage points. It needs positive diluted EPS in four consecutive fiscal years and positive growth. No analyst forecasts are used. Ratio denominators must be positive. Missing or invalid ratios stay absent. Negative cash flow and profit margins remain valid filter values.

Sales-based operating yield spread: multiply selected annual sales by the simple average of operating margins from three consecutive fiscal years. Divide by screen-date EV. Each annual operating margin is operating income divided by revenue. Subtract the latest saved US 10-year Treasury yield on or before the screen date. Enter 5 for a spread of 5 percentage points. Revenue and EV must be positive. Margins and spreads can be negative. Missing years or Treasury values fail only this condition. Latest and dated books use their own screening sessions for the Treasury yield, even when the buy price is delayed. This filter is in current source. The installed runtime needs source publication and an offline rebuild before the filter appears.

All annual inputs match the selected report date. The same 90-day lag, strict availability rule and 800-day age limit apply. A newer report cannot fill missing fields in an older report. Supplier revisions and EPS split treatment can affect results. The existing EBITDA-based stock groups remain the starting universe.

The controls above explain the architecture. They do not select real stocks or run a backtest.

05 / What gets reused

A new setting is not always a new book.

The dated engine saves each buy/sell date pair. It tracks completed stock groups separately. Your final filters and ranks use that group’s prepared records.

Top 50 → Top 100Reuse the same dated books. Select a wider rank range.
Change an existing filterReuse the books. Filter and rank the saved records again.
Choose the other EBITDA metricReuse the books. Both supported metrics are already prepared.
Choose the other stock groupReuse that group if it is complete. Otherwise prepare its records for the same dates. Keep the first group’s records.
Use a new buy/sell date pairPrepare that book if it is not saved.
Run a new seedGenerate new trade dates. Prepare date pairs that are not saved.
Change source data or calculation codeRefresh the affected caches. Rebuild the saved website when needed.
How do I check or download missing data?

Open Manage backtest data from the strategy page. Choose the stock group, symbols and price date range. By default, the panel covers the stocks with saved price files through today, the latest day a download can return. Dated books need these stocks. Check the saved universe, annual financials, stock prices, SPY prices and Treasury yields. Export the check report if needed.

Check saved files→Download missing data→Rebuild prepared data→Open strategy page

A check does not download data or read the API key. Downloads require a button press and use the local FMP key file. The page receives only a key-file presence flag. Raw records already saved are kept. One cache reader validates annual records for both preparation and group inspection. Valid annual rows survive repair of a damaged record. The original financial downloader fills missing symbols. The full-data downloader fills missing endpoint assets for the chosen group. Older trimmed key metrics can be backfilled separately without rewriting baseline inputs. New key-metric downloads also retain every returned field. The price downloader fills ranges outside each saved date span. It does not refresh existing reports or company profiles.

The downloader uses up to 32 parallel requests. It reuses HTTP connections. Compressed responses reduce transferred bytes. The transport requests gzip compression and decodes it before checking the data. Plain responses also work. A shared gate permits at most 45 request starts per second by default. This is 2,700 starts per minute, below this account’s stated allowance of 3,000 calls per minute. A 429 response pauses all workers and lowers the start rate. Retries are bounded and cancellation stops new requests. One owner saves each completed result. Stock and SPY windows cover up to ten years. Treasury windows remain monthly.

Zero or negative adjusted prices are skipped. Usable prices are saved and the batch continues. Skipped dates remain unavailable. The panel warns you and the exported check report lists those dates. These exclusions stay in the content-bound receipt, so later checks still show them. A completed window does not guarantee a price on each date. A response with only excluded prices is recorded as checked but unavailable. It stores no invented prices and does not stop the batch. Missing or nonfinite values still fail. Malformed rows, duplicate usable dates and dates outside the requested window also fail. The error names the affected file and date window.

Successful requests, including empty responses, are recorded in raw/download-coverage.json. Each entry is tied to the saved file by a content hash. Receipts also retain the original saved span and one previous generation. Interrupted publication can match either exact file generation without losing known unfinished windows. Retry reuses a completed window only while that file remains valid and unchanged. Missing or damaged files lose that completion evidence. They can be downloaded again. Legacy entries without a hash do not prove completion. Actual price dates remain visible. A checked range does not guarantee every session. Short histories can come from IPOs or trading stops. Legacy gaps inside an existing span are not repaired automatically. Managed downloads retain their original saved span and each completed window. A late result cannot hide an unfinished earlier window.

The offline rebuild prepares both databases and rebuilds the website. Every research build is a full build. A failure keeps the previous database. Open the strategy page again to load new data. Later saved prices advance latest screening and the dates that custom schedules can use. The separate Full annual financial data download fills missing endpoint assets for the chosen group. It preserves existing valid fields. Each completed endpoint, including an empty response, is bound to its saved content hash. A missing, damaged or changed file must be checked again. Annual statement requests use a 40-report limit; saved coverage is not a promise of complete history.

The panel is served from current source at /data.html. It remains available when essential raw files are missing or invalid. In that case startup opens the panel instead of preparing incomplete data. The tracked report is not one of these files. A saved HTML copy needs the local service to inspect or change files.

One project coordinator protects startup, downloads, rebuilds, fixed schedules and random batches across local server instances. Ownership starts before opening a database. It ends after worker completion and database closure. Nested preparation reuses the same ownership. Cancel waits for active requests or the preparation step. Retry waits check for cancellation. A socket wait has a 15-second timeout. Each request uses a 30-second read deadline and at most three attempts. Completed downloads stay saved. Windows can briefly deny a file replacement while another program reads the file. Atomic cache publication retries these access or sharing locks up to eight times. Total retry waits stay below two seconds. Other file errors fail immediately. Cache ownership and receipt-before-asset ordering stay in place. Terminal shutdown waits for the job to release its locks. These data actions accept only same-origin requests from this computer.

The server saves a development log in data/logs/. The terminal and data panel show the current file. It keeps job results, operation times, provider status, retry counts, affected files and date windows. The development log describes its contents and cleanup.

Which download settings were measured?

The 22 October 2026 experiment used native Windows Python 3.12 and uncached dividend-adjusted stock histories. The temporary experiment did not change the active raw cache. For 16 one-year requests, one pooled worker took 22.09–31.81 seconds. Four workers took 5.57–6.84 seconds. Eight took 3.04–3.54 seconds. Sixteen took 4.06 seconds in one round. These transport tests had no steady start-rate cap.

The policy selected on 22 October had eight workers and a four-starts-per-second cap. It saved 16 one-year histories in 6.56 seconds with 16 HTTP 200 responses and no retries. The serial reference took 42.47 seconds. These runs used the same stock symbols but different historical years. They are samples, not a controlled same-period speedup or a universal optimum.

The experiment also found a Python 3.12 response-reuse problem. The transport now closes each exhausted response before the next request. The empty Treasury probe did not establish annual Treasury coverage, so monthly windows remain. Read the 22 October settings and measurements for that evidence.

The 23 October standalone transport experiment made 1,392 distinct stock/window requests. All returned HTTP 200. Across compressed cases, gzip reduced transferred body bytes by 89.1%. Native Windows Python 3.12.1 averaged 207 calls per minute with eight workers and four starts per second. It averaged 1,207 calls per minute with 32 workers and 45 starts per second, without compression. A larger gzip batch on WSL Python 3.14.4 averaged 2,265 calls per minute with 32 workers. The higher worker counts tested were slower.

That experiment supports the current 32-worker, 45-starts-per-second policy with gzip. Its fresh-pool batches lasted about 2–19 seconds. They used different stocks, historical periods and environments. These are prior transport measurements. They are not new application tests, a controlled application speedup, a sustained-rate test or guaranteed throughput. The full data-panel publication path was not measured. Read the 23 October settings and measurements for the scope and limits.

The source now contains the new transport settings. Restart an existing local server to load the current Python code. Reload the data panel to see the current text. Implementation checks use local provider fixtures and temporary caches. They do not download market data.

Replay can be fast because the work is already saved.

In the reference Windows test, 100 fresh trials took 467 seconds. A replay of those saved books took 5.7 seconds. These are different jobs.

What happens to books from the earlier engine?

Daily refresh checked 6 November 2026. A daily price download keeps every saved dated book that cannot read the new rows. Preparation writes a new daily cache from the previous one. It copies the prices of companies whose file bytes are unchanged and parses only changed files. A book is kept when it reads no price, session or yield on or after the earliest changed day. A book reads nothing after the later of its exit and its entry plus four days. A change to statements, financial inputs, the company set or the book calculation code drops every book. The refreshed cache equals a full build, and each kept book equals a freshly calculated one. The rule lives in backtest/inputs/daily.py; tests/test_schedules.py checks it.

Older daily caches rebuild. Startup prepares daily prices again from saved files. It downloads no market data. Dated books are calculated again when a run needs them. Saved library and queue results stay readable.

History: an earlier version-1/2 in-place upgrade was removed. It could never succeed. Current input fingerprints carry observation evidence that old caches do not have.

The completion marker is saved with the group’s records. An interrupted write cannot mark a half-built group as complete.

What happens if I stop a run?

A fixed-date request saves its new books together. A random batch calculates missing books in parallel. It saves all new books for one trial together, in trial order.

Workers only read data. One parent process saves results in SQLite. A failed trial leaves no partial new books. Unfinished writes roll back. Previously saved books remain. Restart the launcher and replay the saved settings and seed. Completed books can be reused. A stopped request does not resume by itself.

06 / Why new trials take time

Plan shared work.
Calculate books in parallel.

The earlier engine prepared both stock groups for every new date pair. Original prepares only the requested group. Its random batches plan unique missing books upfront. Worker processes calculate ahead. One writer saves each complete trial. Each group still gets both supported metrics and holding returns.

The website runs only Original. The source has no experimental (Numba) engine. The compiled-backtest and parallel-backtest plan summaries keep its measurements.

The earlier engine prepared the broader group for an original-group request. New trials created many extra records.

Prepare only the group you chose. Plan each missing date pair once. Calculate books with read-only workers. Save complete trials through one SQLite writer. An empty group also counts as complete.

Test: original candidate set, top 50, annual random rebalances, 1996–2026. The end date was 20 October 2026. Seed: 20261022. Loading and per-trial saving are included. Common test-only cloning is excluded. The OS file cache was not cleared.

The Windows worker comparison took 103.4, 62.0, 40.9 and 33.2 seconds with 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers. A fresh serial requested-group control took 133.3 seconds. A four-worker check of the applied code took 43.2 seconds, including worker shutdown cleanup. Saved-book replays took about 5.6 seconds. The current default is eight workers for 16 or more missing books, and each worker decodes a company’s financial inputs once. These timings do not measure that default.

All selected holdings, prices, returns and exit statuses matched exactly. The measured gain applies to the original group. Selecting the broader group avoids much less work. Top 100 and P/B-filtered runs were not benchmarked.

Why fewer records help.
The reference test prepared 4,010,439 stock records. The requested-group test prepared 537,906. These are records across periods, not unique companies.

Why shared data is optional.
It added about 12.6 seconds of loading in the 100-trial test. At 24 trials, group-only took 32 seconds. The combined version took 35 seconds.
